mainEntity.name: Can a windscreen seal be replaced without removing the glass?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, yes. Where the failure is in the visible rubber or the external trim and the bond underneath is still sound, the joint can be stripped, cleaned and resealed with the screen left in place. Where the urethane bond itself has failed, or there is corrosion under the edge, the glass has to come out to do the job properly.

mainEntity.name: How do I know the leak is the windscreen and not something else?

acceptedAnswer.text: You often cannot tell from where the water lands. Sunroof drains, door membranes, blocked plenum drains and even a heater core can all wet a footwell. That is why we water test in sections with the trim pulled back: it identifies the entry point instead of assuming it.

mainEntity.name: Why is my car whistling at highway speed after nothing changed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Seals shrink as they age, and a section that has pulled away from a corner or lifted along the top edge lets air through under pressure. It usually appears gradually, then seems sudden because it crosses the threshold where you can hear it over the road. It is worth dealing with, because air getting in means water can too.

mainEntity.name: My leak started after a windscreen replacement elsewhere. What now?

acceptedAnswer.text: Go back to whoever fitted it first, because that is likely a workmanship issue and should be theirs to put right. If that is not an option, we will inspect it, tell you plainly what we find in the aperture, and quote what it takes to make it watertight.

mainEntity.name: Is a leaking windscreen seal dangerous?

acceptedAnswer.text: The water in the carpet is not the safety issue. The bonded windscreen contributes to the structure of the car and helps the passenger airbag deploy against something solid, so a failing bond, rather than just perished trim, is worth taking seriously. It is one of the things we check.

mainEntity.name: How long does the work take?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tracing the leak is often the longest part, because it has to be done properly rather than quickly. The reseal itself is a contained job. What sets your total is curing time before the car should be driven or washed, and we give you that figure on the day.
